Section: Cause
About 10-15% of cases of moyamoya disease are familial, and some cases result from specific genetic mutations.[7] Susceptibility to moyamoya disease-2 (MYMY2; 607151) is caused by variation in the RNF213 gene (613768) on the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q25),[8] although evidence suggests that RNF213 mutation alone is not enough to cause disease.[7] Moyamoya disease-5 (MYMY5; 614042) is caused by mutation in the ACTA2 gene (102620) on the long arm of chromosome 10 (10q23.3); and moyamoya disease-6 with achalasia (MYMY6; 615750) is caused by mutation in the GUCY1A3 gene (139396) on the long arm of chromosome 4 (4q32). Loci for the disorder have been mapped to the short arm of chromosome 3 (MYMY1) and the long arm of chromosome 8 (8q23) (MYMY3; 608796). See also MYMY4 (300845), an X-linked recessive syndromic disorder characterized by moyamoya disease, short stature, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and facial dysmorphism, and linked to q25.3, on chromosome 17.[8] Both familial and sporadic moyamoya cases have unclear molecular causes. Inflammatory cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases have been proposed as contributory factors, though the mechanism and significance of observed associations with these molecules is unknown. Researchers also frequently target known contributors to fibrotic and angiogenic changes, such as FGF and TGF-beta, but no conclusive causes have been found.[7]
Section: Pathophysiology
The disease moyamoya, which is a Japanese mimetic word, gets its characteristic name due to the appearance of smoke on relevant angiographs resultant from the tangle of tiny vessels in response to stenosis. This makes the blood leak out of the arteries, causing pressure to the brain and subsequent headaches. Over the last six decades since the disease was first described,  pathogenesis of moyamoya disease remained elusive, although the gene ring finger protein 213 (RNF213) has been implicated.[9] In September 2021, a south Indian researcher has proposed a pathbreaking theory on moyamoya pathogenesis. Coined the "Mechano-biological theory", the disease has a multifactorial pathogenesis. The authors provide a tangible explanation of the occurrence of moyamoya phenomenon in the idiopathic and syndromic variants of the disease.[10] In short, the authors report that moyamoya disease likely occurs due to a number of factors (e.g., differences in vascular anatomy) that ultimately contribute to broad cerebral blood vessel occlusion and consequent shifts in vessel connections to try to provide blood for the compromised brain.[10] Once it begins, the vascular occlusion tends to continue despite any known medical management. In some people this leads to transient ischemic attacks or repeated strokes with severe functional impairment or even death. In others, the blockage may not cause any symptoms.[11]

0.long_answer: Moyamoya disease 2 is a rare, idiopathic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the intracranial internal carotid arteries and their main branches. This gradual narrowing results in reduced blood flow to the brain and stimulates the formation of a network of small collateral vessels, which on angiographic imaging appears as a 'puff of smoke' (the literal meaning of 'moyamoya' in Japanese). The disease can lead to ischemic strokes, transient ischemic attacks, and hemorrhagic events. Although its precise etiology is not completely understood, it is believed to have a genetic component and has been associated with other conditions such as Down syndrome, sickle cell disease, and neurofibromatosis type 1. Diagnosis is typically achieved through imaging studies such as MRI and angiography, and treatment may include medical management as well as surgical revascularization procedures to improve cerebral blood flow.

Section: Cause
About 10-15% of cases of moyamoya disease are familial, and some cases result from specific genetic mutations.[7] Susceptibility to moyamoya disease-2 (MYMY2; 607151) is caused by variation in the RNF213 gene (613768) on the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q25),[8] although evidence suggests that RNF213 mutation alone is not enough to cause disease.[7] Moyamoya disease-5 (MYMY5; 614042) is caused by mutation in the ACTA2 gene (102620) on the long arm of chromosome 10 (10q23.3); and moyamoya disease-6 with achalasia (MYMY6; 615750) is caused by mutation in the GUCY1A3 gene (139396) on the long arm of chromosome 4 (4q32). Section: Pathophysiology
The disease moyamoya, which is a Japanese mimetic word, gets its characteristic name due to the appearance of smoke on relevant angiographs resultant from the tangle of tiny vessels in response to stenosis. This makes the blood leak out of the arteries, causing pressure to the brain and subsequent headaches. Over the last six decades since the disease was first described,  pathogenesis of moyamoya disease remained elusive, although the gene ring finger protein 213 (RNF213) has been implicated.[9] In September 2021, a south Indian researcher has proposed a pathbreaking theory on moyamoya pathogenesis. Coined the "Mechano-biological theory", the disease has a multifactorial pathogenesis. The authors provide a tangible explanation of the occurrence of moyamoya phenomenon in the idiopathic and syndromic variants of the disease.[10] In short, the authors report that moyamoya disease likely occurs due to a number of factors (e.g., differences in vascular anatomy) that ultimately contribute to broad cerebral blood vessel occlusion and consequent shifts in vessel connections to try to provide blood for the compromised brain.[10] Once it begins, the vascular occlusion tends to continue despite any known medical management. In some people this leads to transient ischemic attacks or repeated strokes with severe functional impairment or even death. In others, the blockage may not cause any symptoms.[11]
